scope_note: All 50 units listed in changed-units.txt for revision 6.2: 39 new or changed (section 1) plus 11 moved or relabeled with unchanged text on the changed lines L21-L23 (section 2). home.md and page.yaml have no changed units. Checked against passages.md only. The extra 'reason' field on each unit gives the basis for the verdict.

units.sentence: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: your school's start date.
units.marker: {analysis: P-007 sets "no later than July 1, 2027", P-008 makes policies due by January 1 each year, and the law doesn't say how the two dates fit; one school's plan (P-054) is the only one in our sources}
units.reason: "no later than July 1, 2027" is verbatim in P-007; P-008 sets policies "By January 1 each year"; nothing in the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) links the two dates; P-054 (Cairo High School) is the only school plan in the passages. P-007 sets only an outer date, so the actual start date really is unknown.
units.problem: Wording only: 'your school's start date' doesn't say start of what and can be read as the first day of school (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: when your school will start the ban.

units.sentence: By July 1, 2027, reaching your child during the school day means contacting the school, which must set emergency-message procedures.
units.evidence_span: Require parents or guardians who need to communicate with their student during the school day to contact the school directly
units.reason: P-011(B) requires policies that make parents contact the school directly; P-008 ('shall adopt ... policies and procedures that, at a minimum') makes the P-011 protocols mandatory, so 'must' is right; P-007 sets July 1, 2027 as the outer date for the high school ban. P-011's protocols belong to the policy due each January 1, so 'By July 1, 2027' is a correct outer bound.
units.problem: Minor: 'emergency-message procedures' is vaguer than the law, which requires protocols that 'Facilitate all emergency communication through school emergency communication management systems and coordinated by school personnel' (P-011(A)). The parent isn't told that emergency messages also go through the school.
units.suggested_fix: ...means contacting the school, which must handle all emergency messages through its emergency system.

units.sentence: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: who pays for phone storage; the law sets aside no money, and we didn't review the state budget.
units.marker: {analysis: each district chooses storage (P-009); no funding or fee provision in the law's full text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061; any state funding would come through the state budget, which is outside our sources}
units.reason: P-009, part of the P-008 list each district and school must adopt, leaves storage methods to them. I found no appropriation, funding or fee language in P-001 to P-019 or P-056 to P-061, which together cover lines 1-106 of the enacted text. The budget point is a stated scope limit.

units.sentence: HB 1009 keeps the school-day device ban House Bill 340 set in 2025 for public school students in kindergarten through 8th grade.
units.evidence_span: no public school student in kindergarten through grade eight shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day
units.reason: P-006 is subsection (b)(1) of the enacted text, archived as existing law left unchanged; P-028 says HB 340, 'signed by the Governor in 2025', banned these devices in K-8.
units.problem: Wording only: 'the school-day device ban House Bill 340 set in 2025' is hard to parse, and 'set in 2025' can be read as the ban starting in 2025, while P-006 says it had to start no later than July 1, 2026 (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: HB 1009 keeps the school-day device ban for kindergarten through 8th grade that a 2025 law, House Bill 340, created.

units.sentence: The bill drops e-readers from the device examples and requires yearly policies.
units.evidence_span: By January 1 each year, each local school system and public school shall adopt, and revise as appropriate, policies and procedures
units.reason: P-021 (prior list) includes 'e-readers' and P-004 (enacted list) doesn't; P-020's one-time 'By January 1, 2026' became P-008's 'By January 1 each year'. 'Requires yearly policies' is a fair shorthand for 'adopt, and revise as appropriate' each year.
units.problem: Missing limit on a K-8 IF-YOU line. P-004's examples are 'not limited to' the list, and the definition still covers any portable device 'capable of transmitting, receiving, or accessing communications, data, or media', so dropping the example doesn't make e-readers allowed. L88 carries this caveat ('that list is not complete'); this line doesn't, so a parent could read it as e-readers now being permitted.
units.suggested_fix: The bill drops e-readers from its list of example devices (the list isn't complete) and requires yearly policies. [P-004, P-021, P-008, P-020]

units.sentence: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: your district's next policy.
units.marker: {analysis: P-008 requires a policy by January 1 each year; no district's policy is in our sources}
units.reason: P-008 sets the yearly deadline; no district or school policy text is among the passages (P-054 is a school news notice, not a policy).

units.sentence: The law takes effect Dec 31, 2026.
units.evidence_span: This Act shall become effective December 31, 2026.
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. P-019 states the date.

units.sentence: From then on, each district's and school's device policy, due by January 1 each year, must cover kindergarten through 12th grade; the first deadline is Jan 1, 2027.
units.marker: {analysis: P-008 sets "By January 1 each year" for policies covering kindergarten through grade twelve, and the law takes effect Dec 31, 2026 (P-019)}
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. The quote is verbatim in P-008, whose item (1) covers 'kindergarten through grade twelve'; the first January 1 after the Dec 31, 2026 effective date (P-019) is Jan 1, 2027.

units.sentence: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027, so the ban must be in place by the 2027-28 school year.
units.marker: {analysis: P-007 sets "no later than July 1, 2027"; a news report put the start in the 2027-28 school year (P-072)}
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. The quote is verbatim in P-007; P-072 says high school restrictions 'would begin in the 2027-28 school year'; a July 1, 2027 outer date puts the ban in place for 2027-28.

units.sentence: The law doesn't say how the January policy deadline fits with the July start date.
units.marker: {analysis: the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) sets both dates (P-008, P-007) without linking them}
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. No provision in the enacted text ties P-008's January 1 deadline to P-007's July 1, 2027 outer date; P-008(1)'s 'subject to exceptions provided for by law' doesn't address timing.
units.problem: Wording only: 'the July start date' presents a 'no later than' deadline as a fixed start date (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: ...fits with the July 1, 2027 deadline to start the ban.

units.sentence: The ban covers personal phones, smartwatches, tablets, headphones and similar devices, but schools can still give students laptops and tablets for schoolwork.
units.evidence_span: smartphones, smartwatches, tablets, headphones, and other devices with functionalities such as wireless communication
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. P-004 gives the device examples; P-017 protects school-provided 'laptops and tablets, for student use for educational purposes'.

units.sentence: Under the law, to "access" a device means to view, hold, wear or otherwise use it, for things like messages, going online, games or music.
units.evidence_span: means viewing, holding, wearing, or otherwise using a device for the purpose of communication, internet access, gaming, recording, listening to music
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. Matches P-003's definition; 'things like' marks the list as partial.

units.sentence: The ban lasts from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, a period the law calls "bell-to-bell."
units.evidence_span: shall include all scheduled instructional time, breaks, transitions, assemblies, and other school related activities
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. P-005 makes the school day the bell-to-bell period; P-002 runs it from the first to the final bell and includes breaks and transitions.

units.sentence: Breaking the rule brings consequences that grow each time, such as warnings, taking the device or notifying parents.
units.evidence_span: shall be subject to progressive consequences in accordance with the local school system's or public school's student code of conduct, including, but not limited to, verbal warnings, confiscation of personal electronic devices, parental notification
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. 'Grow each time' fairly renders 'progressive consequences'; the examples match.

units.sentence: Charter schools and other schools that can usually skip some state rules can't skip this one.
units.evidence_span: shall not be subject to waiver pursuant to Code Section 20-2-82 for a strategic waivers school system, Code Section 20-2-2063.2 or 20-2-2065 for a charter system, Code Section 20-2-2065 for a charter school
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. P-018 bars waivers under the charter, strategic-waivers, completion-school and general waiver sections; 'can usually skip some state rules' is a fair plain reading of having waiver authority.

units.sentence: A student may access a device that their Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires.
units.evidence_span: explicitly mandates the use of a personal electronic device for medical or educational purposes shall be permitted to access the device
units.reason: 'shall be permitted to access' supports 'may access'. The next sentence states the 'as necessary' limit, so the pair is complete.

units.sentence: That access is allowed only "as necessary to fulfill the requirements" of the plan.
units.evidence_span: shall be permitted to access the device as necessary to fulfill the requirements of the respective program or plan
units.reason: The quote is verbatim; 'only' follows because outside this permission the P-007 ban applies.

units.sentence: IEP and Section 504 plans are formal school plans for students with disabilities.
units.marker: {analysis: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources}
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. No passage defines these plans, so this is correctly tagged {analysis} and labeled as not from the sources; the definition is accurate.

units.sentence: Access that another law requires is also allowed.
units.evidence_span: except as otherwise provided in this Code section or required by law
units.reason: Moved unit, text unchanged. P-007's 'or required by law'.

units.sentence: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027.
units.evidence_span: Beginning no later than July 1, 2027, no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day
units.reason: P-007 sets the outer date for grades 9-12.
units.problem: Accurate, but it repeats L21 in the same section. Under 'Decided later by each school district', a deadline the law sets also implies that districts pick the start date, which this revision stopped claiming (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: State the July 1, 2027 date and the 'doesn't say how the dates fit' point once in this section (L21 or L24), not twice.

units.sentence: The law doesn't say how that date fits with the January 1 policy deadline.
units.marker: {analysis: P-008 sets the January 1 deadline; the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) doesn't link the two dates}
units.reason: Correct: no enacted provision links P-008's January 1 deadline to P-007's July 1, 2027 outer date.
units.problem: Duplicates L21's last sentence two bullets earlier in the same section (see framing_issues).

units.sentence: The ban must start no later than July 1, 2027.
units.evidence_span: Beginning no later than July 1, 2027, no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted
units.reason: The deadline is verbatim in P-007.

units.sentence: Policies are due by January 1 each year.
units.evidence_span: By January 1 each year, each local school system and public school shall adopt, and revise as appropriate, policies and procedures
units.reason: P-008 sets the yearly deadline.
units.problem: Wording only: 'Policies' doesn't say whose (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: District and school device policies are due by January 1 each year.

units.sentence: The law doesn't say how the two dates fit.
units.marker: {analysis: the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) sets both dates (P-007, P-008) without linking them}
units.reason: Correct; same finding as L21 and L24.

units.sentence: Our sources include only one school's plan, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.marker: {analysis: P-054 is the only school plan in our sources}
units.reason: P-054 (Cairo High School, June 1, 2026) is the only school or district plan among the passages; P-046 and P-051 report statements about unnamed schools and districts, not plans.

units.sentence: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027, and we found no measured results from Georgia high schools, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.marker: {analysis: P-007; none in the sources reviewed, though a state senator said limits had been used in high schools already (P-046) and one school planned to start in 2026-2027 (P-054)}
units.reason: The deadline matches P-007's 'no later than', replacing the old 'don't have to start until'. No passage reports measured Georgia high school outcomes. P-046 (Harrell: 'It has been done in high schools already') and P-054 (Cairo, 2026-2027) are described accurately.

units.sentence: Check your school's handbook or website, where each district and school must publish the rules.
units.evidence_span: Ensure that parents, guardians, and students are informed of such policies and procedures through student and family handbooks, student codes of conduct, school public websites
units.reason: P-014 supplies the subject and the 'shall' ('Each local school system and public school shall:') that govern P-015(B); 'publish' fairly renders 'ensure ... are informed ... through' those channels. Adding P-014 fixes the old citation's missing 'must'.

units.sentence: Our sources give no phone number, email or meeting for lawmakers.
units.marker: {analysis: none of the archived sources lists one; the General Assembly's lawmaker lookup page held no readable text when we tried to save it on Nov 8, 2026}
units.reason: No passage gives a lawmaker's phone number, email or meeting (P-023 lists sponsors and districts only; P-073 and P-074 are the governor's office). {analysis} fits better than the old {editorial}: this is a checkable claim about the sources.
units.problem: Minor: the failed capture of the lookup page is a process fact that no passage records, so I couldn't check it. Make sure it's logged as a blocked source.

units.sentence: The rules must appear in student and family handbooks, codes of conduct and school websites.
units.evidence_span: through student and family handbooks, student codes of conduct, school public websites, and other common communication channels
units.reason: P-015(B) falls under P-014's 'Each local school system and public school shall', which supports 'must'.

units.sentence: Our sources give no phone numbers or emails for districts.
units.marker: {analysis: none of the archived sources lists one for any district; we found no state directory of districts to save on Nov 8, 2026}
units.reason: No passage gives district contact details (P-054, the only school page, has none). Re-tagging from {editorial} to {analysis} is right.
units.problem: Minor: 'we found no state directory of districts to save' is a process note that no passage records, so I couldn't check it.

units.sentence: Act 395 is the law's number; HB 1009 was the bill's number.
units.marker: {analysis: plain-language note; P-024 gives Act 395, and P-028 and P-054 give the bill number}
units.reason: P-024 lists '05/05/2026 Act 395' but never names HB 1009. P-028 ('HB 1009, sponsored by...') and P-054 ('Georgia House Bill 1009 is a law') do, so the corrected attribution is accurate.

units.sentence: Students who use phones or smartwatches for health apps need an Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan that explicitly requires the device, unless another law requires access.
units.evidence_span: A student whose Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 Plan, or medical plan explicitly mandates the use of a personal electronic device for medical or educational purposes
units.reason: P-013 is the only personal-device exception in the enacted Code section; P-007 adds 'or required by law'; P-004 names smartphones and smartwatches.
units.problem: Minor: unlike L23 and L217, this line drops the limit that plan-based access is only 'as necessary to fulfill the requirements' of the plan (P-013). That limit is part of the cost to these students.
units.suggested_fix: Optional: end with '..., and then only as the plan requires.'

units.sentence: Our sources also quote a public health professor who called parents' emergency concerns valid and said effective policies can address them with rapid parent notification and guaranteed access to phones when needed.
units.marker: {analysis: Gazmararian (P-037)}
units.reason: An accurate paraphrase of P-037 that keeps her qualifiers ('effective' policies 'can' address it) and both conditions (rapid parent notification systems; guaranteed access to phones when needed). She is a professor of epidemiology at the Rollins School of Public Health.
units.problem: Minor: this reports what a source said, so a direct [P-037] citation would let the span check cover it. 'Emergency concerns' is looser than her 'concerns about emergency access', and unlike every other adult speaker in the paragraph she isn't named here (only at L193).
units.suggested_fix: Our sources also quote public health professor Julie Gazmararian, who called parents' concerns about emergency access valid and said effective policies can address them with rapid parent notification and guaranteed access to phones when needed. [P-037]

units.sentence: That summary doesn't say which effects were larger, or whether Florida's bans covered the whole school day, as Georgia's will.
units.marker: {analysis: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't say; Georgia's rule covers the whole day (P-002, P-007)}
units.reason: The five abstract passages say only 'The effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings' without naming the outcomes, and they never describe how much of the day the bans covered. Georgia's ban is bell-to-bell.
units.problem: Minor: the 'whole day' chain needs P-005 ('School day' means the bell-to-bell period), because P-002 and P-007 alone don't connect 'during the school day' to bell-to-bell. Optional precision, also at L155 and L203: the abstract says 'The effects' without qualification, so 'doesn't say whether that holds for each effect' is more exact than 'which effects', which presumes only some were larger.
units.suggested_fix: Tag: Georgia's rule covers the whole day (P-002, P-005, P-007).

units.sentence: We found no measured results from Georgia high schools yet.
units.marker: {analysis: none in the sources reviewed, though a state senator said limits had been used in high schools already (P-046); Georgia's high school ban must start no later than July 1, 2027 (P-007)}
units.reason: Correct. The tag now matches P-007's 'no later than' instead of the old 'isn't required until'.

units.sentence: That summary doesn't say which effects were larger: test scores, absences or suspensions.
units.marker: {analysis: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't say}
units.reason: The abstract's last sentence (P-040) doesn't name which of the three outcomes listed in P-038 was larger. The caveat is applied equally here (supporting card) and at L203 (opposing card).

units.sentence: Whether Georgia high schools will see results like Florida's, since we found no Georgia high school results yet.
units.marker: {analysis: none in the sources reviewed; Georgia's high school ban must start no later than July 1, 2027 (P-007)}
units.reason: Correct; the deadline is now stated as 'no later than'.

units.sentence: Teens' mental health and in-person friendships would improve, supporters say.
units.evidence_span: Improved in-person social interactions 71.2 (2.6) Improved mental health and wellbeing
units.reason: Mental health: P-036 ('a mental health issue'), P-071 ('ease anxiety') and P-034. 'In-person' is now supported by P-034, the reasons given by parents who support a ban; P-051 adds 'less isolation' and 'feel further apart'.
units.problem: Minor: no source says 'friendships'. P-034 says 'in-person social interactions' and P-051 says 'less isolation'. A fair plain-language summary, but slightly narrower than the sources.
units.suggested_fix: Optional: 'Teens' mental health and in-person social lives would improve, supporters say.'

units.sentence: A study in England found no evidence of better well-being among 12- to 15-year-olds at schools that barred phone use for fun.
units.evidence_span: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents
units.reason: Scope is correct: 30 English secondary schools (P-041), ages 12-15 (P-042), restrictive meaning 'recreational phone use is not permitted' (P-041), and no evidence of a well-being difference (P-042, P-043).

units.sentence: The English study also found no evidence of less phone or social media use overall at its strict schools.
units.evidence_span: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use
units.reason: Matches P-043. P-042 shows lower use only during school time, with no evidence of differences on weekdays or weekends. L167 reports the during-school drop, so the card isn't one-sided.

units.sentence: No one in the sources we reviewed disputed that Georgia's phone rules are working.
units.marker: {analysis: none of the archived statements about Georgia disputes it; teacher Darryl Adams's concerns were about enforcement, emergencies and older students (P-047 to P-049); the English study's authors wrote about schools in England (P-043)}
units.reason: Adams's statements (P-047 to P-049) and the survey opponents' reasons (P-035) don't dispute that Georgia's rules work, and the English study's caution is drawn from English schools, not Georgia.
units.problem: Minor citation detail in the tag: P-043 doesn't mention England; P-041 ('30 English secondary schools') does.
units.suggested_fix: Tag: ...wrote about schools in England (P-041, P-043).

units.sentence: Harrell's quoted passage doesn't name the high schools or say how their success was measured.
units.marker: {analysis: based on P-046, with P-044 naming her as a state senator}
units.reason: P-046 names no school and gives no measure; P-044 says 'State Sen. Sally Harrell'. Adams gets a matching caveat at L194, so the two sides are treated alike.
units.problem: Wording only: 'quoted passage' is internal jargon for readers (see framing_issues).
units.suggested_fix: The news report quoting Harrell doesn't name the high schools or say how their success was measured.

units.sentence: The law requires each district's and school's policy to set clear protocols that send all emergency communication through school emergency systems, coordinated by school staff.
units.evidence_span: Establish clear communication protocols that: (A) Facilitate all emergency communication through school emergency communication management systems and coordinated by school personnel
units.reason: P-008 makes the P-011 protocols required for each local school system and public school. The paraphrase keeps 'all', 'clear', the school systems and staff coordination.
units.problem: Minor: 'send' is a little firmer than the law's verb, 'Facilitate'.
units.suggested_fix: Optional: '...protocols that handle all emergency communication through school emergency systems...'

units.sentence: The law doesn't require the "rapid parent notification systems" or the "guaranteed access to phones when needed" that Gazmararian named, and her words don't say whose phones.
units.marker: {analysis: no such requirement in the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061); her words are from P-037}
units.reason: Both quotes are verbatim in P-037. The enacted text routes emergency communication through school systems (P-011) but sets no speed or parent-notification requirement and guarantees no phone access (the only exceptions are P-013's plan and P-007's 'required by law'). P-037 doesn't say whose phones.

units.sentence: Districts can add faster parent alerts, because the law sets minimum rules, but by our reading they can't let students use their own phones in an emergency unless a student's disability or medical plan, or another law, requires access.
units.marker: {analysis: P-008 says policies must "at a minimum" include its list; P-007 allows access only as the law provides, P-011 sends all emergency communication through school systems, and the only device exception is a plan that requires one (P-013)}
units.reason: 'at a minimum' is verbatim in P-008, and no enacted provision gives an emergency exception for personal devices. The conclusion is hedged ('by our reading') and keeps both exceptions (a plan, another law).

units.sentence: The quoted passage doesn't say when Adams's lockdown happened or what phone rules applied.
units.marker: {analysis: based on P-049, with P-047 naming him as a teacher}
units.reason: P-049 gives no date or phone rules; P-047 names him as a teacher. Dropping the old 'one family's experience' leaves the caveats even with Harrell's at L182.
units.problem: Wording only: P-049 is reported speech with no direct quote, so 'quoted passage' is inexact as well as jargon. 'Adams's lockdown' reads as if he was locked down; it was two of his daughters.
units.suggested_fix: The news report doesn't say when the lockdown Adams described happened or what phone rules applied.

units.sentence: The study's summary says the bans' effects were larger in middle and high schools, where more students own smartphones.
units.evidence_span: The effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings where student smartphone ownership is more common
units.reason: A faithful paraphrase. Adding it to card 5 mirrors card 1 (L155), and the next sentence's caveat stops it from implying that the suspension effect was larger.

units.sentence: That summary doesn't say which effects were larger: test scores, absences or suspensions.
units.marker: {analysis: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't say}
units.reason: Same as L155; the caveat is applied evenly to both cards.

units.sentence: Whether Georgia high schools will see a short-term rise in suspensions like Florida's, since we found no Georgia high school results yet.
units.marker: {analysis: none in the sources reviewed; Georgia's high school ban must start no later than July 1, 2027 (P-007)}
units.reason: Correct; it matches L159's wording on the supporting card.

units.sentence: The law lets a student access a device that their Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires, but only "as necessary to fulfill the requirements" of that plan.
units.evidence_span: explicitly mandates the use of a personal electronic device for medical or educational purposes shall be permitted to access the device as necessary to fulfill the requirements
units.reason: The quote is verbatim, and both the exception and its limit are stated.

framing_issues.text: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: your school's start date.
framing_issues.issue: Vague: 'start date' doesn't say start of what. A student can read it as the first day of school rather than the day the ban starts.

framing_issues.text: contacting the school, which must set emergency-message procedures
framing_issues.issue: Vague on the IF-YOU line where it matters most: it doesn't tell parents that all emergency communication must go through the school's emergency system, coordinated by staff (P-011(A)).

framing_issues.text: The bill drops e-readers from the device examples
framing_issues.issue: Implies e-readers are now allowed for K-8 students. The examples are 'not limited to' the list (P-004), and L88 adds 'that list is not complete', but this IF-YOU line leaves that out.

framing_issues.text: keeps the school-day device ban House Bill 340 set in 2025
framing_issues.issue: Hard to parse ('ban House Bill 340 set'), above the grade 6-8 target. 'Set in 2025' can be read as the ban starting in 2025; P-006 says it had to start no later than July 1, 2026.

framing_issues.text: fits with the July start date
framing_issues.issue: Calls a 'no later than' deadline a start date.

framing_issues.text: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027. ... The law doesn't say how that date fits with the January 1 policy deadline.
framing_issues.issue: Repeats L21's last two sentences in the same section, and L29 says it a third time, against the concise, phone-first tenet. Placed under 'Decided later by each school district', a deadline set by the law also implies that districts pick the start date, which the page no longer claims.

framing_issues.text: Policies are due by January 1 each year.
framing_issues.issue: Vague reference: it doesn't say whose policies (each district's and school's device policy).

framing_issues.text: Our sources also quote a public health professor
framing_issues.issue: Uneven naming: every other adult speaker in this paragraph is named, but she isn't until L193. 'Emergency concerns' is looser than her 'concerns about emergency access'.
Undefined term: 'passage' is internal jargon, and 'Harrell's passage' suggests she wrote it, when it's a news report quoting her.

framing_issues.text: The quoted passage doesn't say when Adams's lockdown happened
framing_issues.issue: Same jargon. P-049 has no direct quote of Adams, and 'Adams's lockdown' reads as if he was locked down; it was two of his daughters.
